title: Consumption site funding and 2025 paramedic response targets
subtitle: Delegations on harm reduction, HART hub applications, unsupervised-site legislation concerns, paramedic offload delays, and immunization funding shortfall.
overview: The committee recommended that Regional Council urge the Ontario government to keep funding all operating consumption and treatment sites beyond the proposed March 2025 end date, and to maintain funding for planned HART hubs. As amended during the meeting, the motion also asks the province not to legislate against temporary urgent public health needs sites {{vote:m1}}. It would be forwarded to the Premier, the Ministers of Finance and Health, and other municipalities with such sites. Staff said they are working to a tight deadline on a HART hub application that could include a Cambridge satellite.

The committee also recommended approving the 2025 Response Time Performance Plan for paramedic services {{vote:m2}}. It keeps the compliance targets but loosens response times for lower-urgency calls so crews can focus on sudden cardiac arrest and the most critical patients. Staff reported that ambulance offload delays have improved since January, and that Code Red and Code Yellow terminology ends on November 1, 2024.

The committee received reports on immunization compliance and paramedic performance for information. Members noted that provincial cost sharing for public health is only 68%. These recommendations go to Regional Council for a final decision. The committee later met in closed session on a legal matter and a personal matter.

decisions.detail: The committee recommended that Council urge the province to continue funding all operating consumption and treatment sites past March 2025, maintain HART hub funding, and not legislate against temporary urgent public health needs sites {{vote:m1}}.

The committee recommended approving the 2025 plan under the Ambulance Act, with sudden cardiac arrest at 6 minutes or less 70% of the time and CTAS 1 to 5 targets of 8, 10, 15, 20 and 25 minutes {{vote:m2}}.

debate: Delegates and several councillors said the Kitchener site reverses overdoses, builds trust, and connects people to health and social services. Some described a cleaner, safer neighbourhood nearby. Supporters said closure would raise calls to paramedics, police and hospitals.

Staff said the HART hub model does not allow supervised consumption, safe supply or needle exchange. Closing sites will likely raise emergency calls, though costs cannot yet be quantified. Councillors backed a "yes and" approach, wanting harm reduction inside the hub model rather than in competition with it.

Opponents of the motion said the province is unlikely to reverse course and that efforts should go toward more HART hub and treatment funding. One councillor said attention should go to wider drug use across the region, better data, and prevention for young people. Another raised an ethical concern about informed consent. Another councillor asked whether the motion should focus on Waterloo Region rather than all of Ontario.

On paramedic response times, staff said the new plan prioritizes the most critical patients so crews can respond to them faster, and lets lower-acuity calls wait longer. A councillor asked about Cambridge response times. Staff said density, geography and low call volumes in smaller municipalities affect the figures, and that Cambridge improved over the same period last year.
